back: A new or improved product developed because consumers demand it — the need comes first. Lower risk, e.g. reusable water bottles.
A development in technology, materials or manufacturing creates a product consumers did not know they wanted. Higher risk, e.g. touchscreens.

front: Effects of automation and robotics on industry
back: Higher output, consistency and quality and fewer dangerous jobs — but fewer manual roles and large upfront investment.
CNC and CAM equipment can be reprogrammed for a different product, so factories respond quickly to changes in demand.
Making products only when ordered — reduces the cost of holding stock and waste from unsold goods.

front: How new technology helps small enterprises
back: Cheap 3D printers, subscription CAD and online manufacturing lower barriers to entry; crowdfunding proves demand; selling direct reaches a global market.
Proving demand and raising money from the public before committing to production, reducing financial risk.
Overlays computer-generated images onto a view of the real world, e.g. placing a virtual product in your home before buying.
Replaces the real world with a computer-generated environment viewed through a headset — walking through products before they exist, virtual ergonomic testing, safe training.
The designer enters constraints (loads, materials, size, process) and AI-driven CAD produces many possible solutions, often lighter and more efficient.
Who owns an AI-generated design, and designers becoming too reliant on the software's judgement.
Quick modification and re-testing, simulation reduces physical prototypes, professional 3D presentation, direct transfer to CAM, cloud collaboration.
Expensive software and hardware, significant training, early ideas often quicker by hand, files can be lost, hacked or copied, over-reliance limits originality.
A focused beam cuts or engraves sheet material very accurately with little waste. Suits acrylic, plywood, MDF and card; needs extraction; PVC must never be cut (toxic fumes).
Builds products in layers — complex shapes and one-offs, rapid prototyping, little waste — but slow for volume and weaker along layer lines.
3D printing with smart or programmable materials so the object changes shape or function over time in response to a stimulus. The fourth dimension is time.
Being developed for stents, pipes that change diameter and self-adjusting textiles; still experimental, expensive and unproven long term.
Identical quality, continuous running, accurate repeats of complex shapes, quick changeover, efficient use of material.
High purchase and maintenance costs, fewer skilled manual jobs, needs trained programmers, errors repeat across a batch, small runs may not justify set-up.
